newsitem.title: UK: ATHLETICS-MOORCROFT HAS HARD JOB TO MAKE BRITAIN GREAT.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-MOORCROFT HAS HARD JOB TO MAKE BRITAIN GREAT.

text.p: Former world record holder David Moorcroft has taken on the tough job of trying to make Britain successful in athletics again.

Moorcroft, who broke the 5,000 metres world record in 1982 and was part of the country's golden era of middle-distance and distance running in the 1980s, was named as the new chief executive of the British Athletic Federation (BAF) on Thursday.

The 44-year-old Moorcroft, who has been a successful television commentator since he retired from competition, will take control of a sport which was plunged deep into crisis when former Olympic sprinter Peter Radford unexpectedly quit as executive chairman last January.

Britain is in danger of losing its standing in world athletics and is desperately looking for big new names to replace the likes of former Olympic sprint champion Linford Christie and hurdler Colin Jackson who now seem to have past their best.
The country used to be the envy of the world with an array of class middle-distance runners like Seb Coe, Steve Ovett and Steve Cram in the 1980s.
But recently it has suffered with high-profile doping cases and a much-publicised row over appearance money involving major stars.
In addition BAF has lost a great deal of money through falling attendances and television revenue.

Moorcroft, who takes up office in October, is an amiable character who has been a member of his local club in Coventry all his life. Eloquent and diplomatic, he has a reputation for being one of the sport's "nice guys".
But he made it clear on Thursday that he would be prepared to take some tough decisions.
"You can be a pleasant person but also strong and tough," he said. "I don't shirk from making difficult decisions."
Moorcroft said he hoped to bridge the gap between the elite areas of the sport and the grass roots level and make sure talented youngsters could progress to the international stage.
Improving communications within the sport is also an important issue, especially after a difficult week.
On Tuesday Olympic silver medallist Roger Black launched a fierce attack on British athletics chiefs after they left him out of the individual 400 metres for next month's world championships.
Black, one of the country's most prominent athletes who last month took over from Christie as captain of the national team, was livid that he had learned of the decision first in the British media.
